title: Millet: Protein, Carbohydrates, and Minerals

seo.title: Millet: Protein, Carbohydrates, and Minerals
seo.meta_description: Cooked millet provides about 119 calories, 3.5 g protein, and 24 g carbohydrate per 100 g, plus magnesium and phosphorus.
seo.search_intent: Understand millet nutrition and how it compares with other grains.

excerpt: Millet is a naturally gluten-free cereal that, cooked, provides roughly 119 calories, 3.5 g protein, and 24 g carbohydrate per 100 g. Its cooked fiber content is modest, while dry millet contributes minerals including magnesium, phosphorus, and manganese.
content_html:
“Millet” does not refer to one single species but to a group of small-seeded cereal grains eaten for thousands of years in many regions. Nutritionally, millet behaves more like rice, couscous, or sorghum than like a legume: carbohydrate is the dominant macronutrient. Its value is variety, an adaptable texture, and naturally gluten-free grain options.

What cooked millet provides

Per 100 g cookedApprox.
Calories119
Protein3.5 g
Carbohydrate24 g
Fiber~1–1.5 g

The table makes clear why millet should not be marketed as an unusually high-protein grain. Its 3.5 g per 100 g cooked is in the same general range as other cooked grains; a 180 g serving would provide roughly 6.3 g protein.

Dry millet looks much more concentrated for a simple reason

The dry grain contains little water, so protein, carbohydrate, and minerals are concentrated into 100 g. During cooking it absorbs liquid and the same nutrients are spread through more weight.

The same logic applies to minerals such as magnesium, phosphorus, manganese, and copper. Compare dry millet with dry grains or cooked millet with cooked grains, not across different hydration states.

Millet is naturally gluten-free

Millet belongs to cereal grains that do not naturally contain gluten. For celiac disease, cross-contact still matters in flour, flakes, and processed mixes.

Pure millet flour does not have the botanical gluten issue of wheat, but a food advertised as “with millet” may contain other ingredients and needs to be checked separately.

Water changes the texture dramatically

With a moderate amount of liquid and a rest after cooking, millet can remain fairly separate for salads or side dishes. With more water and longer cooking, it becomes creamy and porridge-like, almost like polenta.

That flexibility is useful in the kitchen and also explains why two cooked millet dishes may not have the same nutrient density per 100 g: their water content can be very different.

What millet really adds to a diet

Millet's main value is not a spectacular single nutrient number; it is another useful whole-grain option. It supplies carbohydrate, some protein, and minerals, and can be paired with legumes, vegetables, dairy, eggs, fish, or meat depending on the meal.

How to cook millet so its nutrition is easy to use in real meals

Millet can end up fluffy, creamy or almost porridge-like depending on the amount of water and how much it is stirred. For a loose side dish, rinse the grain, use a moderate amount of water and let it simmer gently without constant stirring. For a softer breakfast-style texture, add more liquid and cook longer. Toasting the dry millet in the pan before adding water can deepen the flavor without materially changing its macronutrient profile. These changes in texture matter because they determine whether millet works as a rice substitute, a breakfast cereal or a base for patties and casseroles.

Like other whole seeds and grains, millet contains phytate, a natural compound that can bind some minerals during digestion. That does not make millet nutritionally poor, and a varied diet normally provides minerals from many sources. Soaking, fermenting and some cooking methods can reduce phytate to varying degrees, while pairing plant foods with vitamin C-rich vegetables can support iron absorption from the meal. The bigger nutritional picture is therefore the whole plate rather than one isolated mineral number in a database.

Millet is naturally gluten-free, but the same cross-contact caution applies as with other gluten-free grains. People who need strict gluten avoidance should choose products handled in a way that minimizes contamination with wheat, barley or rye. Once cooked, millet can be paired with lentils, beans, yogurt, eggs, fish or tofu to raise the protein content of the meal, since millet itself is not an unusually concentrated protein food. Its main advantage is variety: it offers a different texture and flavor while contributing carbohydrate, some fiber, protein and minerals. Used that way, it is a useful staple rather than a nutritional miracle food.

Cooked millet keeps for several days in the refrigerator when cooled promptly and stored covered, which makes it useful for batch cooking. Reheat it with a splash of water for a softer texture, or chill it completely before using it in salads where separated grains work better.

faq.question: How much protein is in cooked millet?
Is millet low-carb?
faq.answer: No. Cooked millet contains roughly 24 g carbohydrate per 100 g.
